paragraph_patches.before: Disagreement among instance segmenters can reflect missing foreground or different partitions of shared foreground. These mechanisms need not identify the same errors. We examine their separation in three-model segmentation of peripelvic fractures on CT. On 40 development scans, we quantify component contributions and test controlled merge, split, omission, boundary, and count-replication perturbations. A separate 100-scan evaluation compares 12 fixed scores using case-clustered bootstrap intervals. Joint-entropy normalization improves the combined score over foreground disagreement and mean entropy for pooled merge/split ranking: area under the risk--coverage curve decreases from 0.4942 and 0.6358 to 0.3311. However, the original partition-only component performs better (0.2720). Supplementary one-to-one and significant-overlap endpoints remove clear evidence of that component's advantage over the combined score. Count-based fusion also lacks a clear development gain. Shared omissions can yield zero disagreement, and fixed-budget review benefits remain uncertain. The findings support component-aware, endpoint-specific evaluation of instance disagreement rather than a universal ranking advantage or demonstrated clinical review savings.
paragraph_patches.after: Disagreement among instance segmenters can reflect missing foreground or different groupings of the same foreground. These mechanisms need not identify the same errors. We study their separation in three-model segmentation of peripelvic fractures on CT. Controlled perturbations and component analysis use 40 development scans; a separate 100-scan evaluation compares 12 fixed scores. Dividing partition disagreement by joint entropy, rather than by the logarithm of voxel count, increases its contribution to the combined score. For pooled merge/split detection, this combined score achieves area under the risk--coverage curve 0.3311, compared with 0.4942 for foreground disagreement and 0.6358 for mean entropy; lower values indicate fewer errors among retained predictions. A partition-only score nevertheless performs better (0.2720). Its advantage is no longer clear under supplementary one-to-one and significant-overlap failure definitions. Unanimously missing bones can receive zero disagreement, and results at fixed review budgets do not establish reliable benefit. These findings show why component controls and explicit failure definitions are necessary when evaluating prediction disagreement for quality control.

paragraph_patches.before: This study makes three contributions: it separates and tests the mechanisms of foreground and partition disagreement; compares both components and their combination against strong controls on a case-disjoint evaluation set; and examines how matching conventions, omission, and review cost change the conclusions. It reports successful contrasts together with stronger baselines and unsuccessful fusion attempts. The aim is to characterize when disagreement is informative, without assuming that its combined form must be superior.
paragraph_patches.after: This study addresses three questions. What changes when foreground disagreement is separated from disagreement about fragment grouping? Does changing the partition normalization improve failure detection against strong component controls? Do those conclusions persist when failure definitions and review budgets change? We answer these questions using controlled perturbations, a separate evaluation cohort, and supplementary endpoint analyses. The contribution is an evidence-based account of what the scores measure and where they fail, rather than a claim that combining components must improve every quality-control task.

paragraph_patches.after: Three ensemble members used the same public two-stage STU-Net segmentation backend and initial 40-case training selection, with three different random seeds. The implementation used nnU-Net 2.5.1 infrastructure~\cite{isensee2021} and a fixed, patched version of the public implementation~\cite{abbc}. paragraph_patches.after: Controlled tests used 20 development CTs (10 per scan type; 40 bones), with unchanged labels, permuted labels, merges, splits, fragment removals, and boundary changes generated independently from reference copies. Each intervention isolates a known change: merging two fragments alters their grouping even if the foreground stays identical, whereas removing foreground changes presence. Eligibility was retained explicitly. Count replication multiplied every entry in a partition contingency table by $r\in\{1,2,4,8,16\}$ without changing its probabilities. VI, joint entropy, presence, and overlap weight should therefore remain fixed, while $Q_{\rm vox}$ decreases with $\log(r|C|)$. This isolates the denominator's algebra; it does not test model robustness to CT resampling. Merge severity was compared within fixed eligible bone cohorts so that changes in the sample could not masquerade as a severity response.

paragraph_patches.after: On the 80 development bones, changing from voxel-count to joint-entropy normalization increased the median weighted partition term from 0.001164 to 0.032116. Raw VI averaged over model pairs was at most $10^{-12}$ in 27/80 bones, however. Normalization therefore changes component scale but cannot create disagreement where the models already give the same grouping.

paragraph_patches.after: The partition-only control was stronger than the combined score on the original structural endpoint (Table~\ref{tab:main}). Voxel-normalized partition disagreement achieved AURC 0.2720, compared with 0.3311 for the joint-entropy combined score, and the paired interval favored the partition-only control. A larger partition contribution therefore does not guarantee a better ranking: adding presence can change which errors receive highest priority. Hungarian matching disagreement had the lowest point AURC for the original $1-F_1$ endpoint, showing that the strongest score also depends on whether failure means incorrect grouping or poor instance detection.

paragraph_patches.before: The supplementary evaluation reconciled all original per-model risks before recomputing matching-based endpoints on the same 140 evaluation CTs. On held-out member-mean risk, FA-v2's disadvantage to partition-v1 was clear for the original M+S definition, but not for one-to-one $1-F_1$ or either significant-overlap definition (Table~\ref{tab:sensitivity}). These changes do not show FA-v2 superiority. They show that the component advantage depends on what is counted as a structural failure. Absolute AURCs across different risk definitions are not changes in segmentation quality.
paragraph_patches.after: The supplementary evaluation reproduced the original per-model risks before recomputing alternative endpoints on the same 40 development and 100 evaluation CTs. For the separate evaluation cohort, the joint-entropy combined score was worse than voxel-normalized partition disagreement under the original merge/split definition, but this disadvantage was no longer clear for one-to-one $1-F_1$ or either significant-overlap definition (Table~\ref{tab:sensitivity}). The segmentations and scores stayed fixed; only the definition of failure changed. The result therefore shows endpoint dependence, not improved segmentation or superiority of the combined score under the alternative definitions. The different risk scales also prevent comparing absolute AURCs across endpoint definitions.

Every ensemble disagreement score was zero, while missing-volume risk was one and merge/split risk was zero. paragraph_patches.before: The decomposition resolves two issues that can otherwise be conflated. First, a count-dependent denominator can numerically suppress partition disagreement. The replication test isolates this effect without inference or image resampling. Second, correcting that suppression does not ensure the preferred ordering of clinically relevant failures. Partition-v1 remained stronger on the original structural endpoint, while supplementary matching rules changed the relative evidence. This agrees with problem-aware validation recommendations~\cite{reinke2024,maier2024}: scale, evaluation unit, and failure definition require separate controls.
paragraph_patches.after: The experiments separate score magnitude from failure-detection value. Replication shows that a voxel-count denominator can suppress partition disagreement without any change in fragment proportions. The separate evaluation cohort shows that removing this suppression helps the combined score against foreground controls, while leaving a partition-only control stronger on the original structural endpoint. Supplementary matching rules then change that comparison without changing any prediction. In practice, a quality-control score should therefore be chosen for a stated failure definition, rather than because one component has a larger numerical range. This agrees with problem-aware validation recommendations~\cite{reinke2024,maier2024}: scale, evaluation unit, and failure definition need separate controls.

paragraph_patches.after: The main limitations are one segmentation-backend family, only three ensemble members, limited femur precision, and no independent replication of the supplementary endpoint analyses. Pooled bone weighting differs from equal-CT review cost, so pooled ranking gains cannot be translated directly into a percentage of scans saved from review. Prediction cleanup can remove small components while reference annotations retain small fragments. Significant-overlap thresholds were diagnostic choices rather than clinically validated cutoffs. Clinical correction, decision consequences, reading time, and external-dataset transfer were not evaluated. The findings consequently characterize the behavior of disagreement scores in this setting; they do not establish clinical savings or safety across datasets.

paragraph_patches.before: Separating foreground presence from shared-foreground partition disagreement clarifies both a normalization mechanism and its limits. The combined normalized score improved pooled held-out ranking over presence and entropy, but a partition-only baseline was stronger under the original structural endpoint. That advantage was endpoint-dependent, small learned fusions did not establish improvement, and shared omissions remained a blindspot. Instance-segmentation quality control should therefore report component controls, matching sensitivity, and review-budget outcomes together.
paragraph_patches.after: Separating foreground presence from shared-foreground partition disagreement explains both a normalization effect and its limits. Joint-entropy normalization improved the combined score's pooled failure ranking over presence and entropy, but voxel-normalized partition disagreement was stronger under the original structural endpoint. That advantage depended on the failure definition, while shared omissions remained invisible to disagreement. Quality-control evaluations should report component controls, matching sensitivity, and fixed-budget outcomes together, because none of these measurements alone establishes reliable review benefit.
